question: How should reliability of tool-using language-model agents be operationalized beyond mean task success, and what do repeated-run consistency, perturbation robustness, confidence calibration, and safety reveal about contemporary agents?

key_findings.claim: Mean task accuracy is not a sufficient reliability measure; the paper separates consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety into twelve metrics.
key_findings.evidence: The framework measures outcome, trajectory-distribution, sequence, and resource consistency; fault, environment, and prompt robustness; calibration, AUROC, and Brier predictability; and compliance and harm safety.

anchors.section: 3 Operationalizing Reliability for AI Agents, Table 2

key_findings.claim: Agent capability rose substantially over the evaluated release timeline, while aggregate reliability improved much less and individual dimensions remained uneven.
key_findings.evidence: Across 15 models on GAIA and a cleaned tau-bench subset, the longitudinal analysis reports strong accuracy gains but persistent outcome inconsistency, prompt sensitivity, and severe confidence errors on tau-bench.

anchors.section: G.2 Reliability trends over time and accuracy, Figure 8

key_findings.claim: Larger or more capable agents need not be more consistent, and reasoning-focused models improve reliability less than their accuracy gains might suggest.
key_findings.evidence: The cross-model comparisons include larger models with lower consistency and show that reasoning variants increase capability without proportionate improvement across the reliability dimensions.

anchors.section: G.6 Level-stratified analysis on GAIA, Figure 20

key_findings.claim: Benchmark defects materially alter reliability conclusions, not merely headline accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: After prior auditing identified errors in 24 of the original 50 tau-bench airline tasks, the authors restrict their evaluation to the verified 26-task airline subset and compare it with the full 50-task airline set. No retail tasks are part of the reported experiment.

key_findings.claim: The reported overall reliability score is not a holistic deployment-readiness score because it omits safety and compresses predictability to Brier score alone.
key_findings.evidence: The aggregation averages equal-weight consistency, robustness, and predictability components, explicitly excludes safety, and defines aggregate predictability using only Brier score despite reporting calibration and AUROC separately.

key_findings.claim: Outcome consistency can reward an agent that fails every run and can fall when an incapable agent begins to succeed occasionally.
key_findings.evidence: The metric C_out=(2p-1)^2 is one at both p=0 and p=1 and zero near p=0.5. This deliberately separates repeatability from capability, but it creates a non-monotonic deployment interpretation if read without success rate.

key_findings.claim: The fault-tolerance protocol partly measures recovery implemented by the evaluation wrapper rather than by the agent.
key_findings.evidence: The wrapper injects tool-call faults with probability 0.2 and applies an internal recovery probability that increases with retry count, so observed task recovery conflates agent behavior with harness behavior.

key_findings.claim: Evaluator independence is incomplete for prompt robustness and safety.
key_findings.evidence: GPT-4o generates the five paraphrases once and also judges safety compliance and severity; the paper does not report a human semantic-equivalence audit for paraphrases or human inter-rater validation of the safety judge.

key_findings.claim: The study measures inference-repeat uncertainty but does not isolate training-seed uncertainty, compute effects, or scaffold effects.
key_findings.evidence: Each model-task condition uses five runs, generally at temperature zero except provider-controlled reasoning defaults, with one benchmark-specific scaffold. Providers, APIs, reasoning modes, and budgets differ across models.

key_findings.claim: The real-incident analysis supports plausibility, not prospective predictive validity.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix retrospectively maps known public agent incidents to framework dimensions and says the metrics could have identified vulnerabilities; no preregistered threshold predicts unseen production failures.

anchors.section: G.1 Connection to Real-World Failures, Table 7

key_findings.claim: Fault and environment robustness largely saturate under the chosen perturbations, so those two metrics provide little model separation in this experiment.
key_findings.evidence: Scores cluster near one on tau-bench and remain high on GAIA, while prompt robustness varies substantially. The authors explicitly say their perturbation suite covers only a limited slice of deployment shifts, making this a negative/null result for the current fault and environment stress tests rather than evidence that the agents are generally robust.

key_findings.claim: Selective prediction largely fails on the verified tau-bench subset despite modest improvement in aggregate calibration.
key_findings.evidence: All agents are severely overconfident on tau-bench, and most accuracy–coverage curves are indistinguishable from the random baseline; only Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.7 show modest selective-prediction ability. This separates population-level calibration from useful per-task failure ranking.

key_findings.claim: Safety improves in newer frontier models, but financial-accuracy violations remain the most common measured failure and rare severe violations persist.
key_findings.evidence: The most capable models from each provider have the highest compliance and lower violation rates; most observed violations are low-to-moderate severity, high-severity cases are rare, and incorrect charges or refunds are the dominant constraint category on tau-bench.

key_findings.claim: The severity labels shown to the safety judge do not match the score bands used for the reported harm metric.
key_findings.evidence: The prompt labels 1.5–3 as low, 3.5–5.5 as medium, 6–8 as high, and 8.5–10 as critical. The subsequent metric implementation instead maps [1.5,5.5] to low, (5.5,8] to medium, and (8,10] to high, collapsing critical and shifting the prompt's medium/high cases down one weight level without an explanation.

anchors.section: F.3.5 Error Severity Analysis Prompt and metric mapping

key_findings.claim: Predictability scores are not always direct measurements of the agent's expressed confidence because parse failures trigger an evaluator heuristic.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix F.3.4 says an unparsable numeric response is replaced by a fallback based on the execution error count. For those cases, calibration, Brier, and discrimination partly measure the harness's hand-coded proxy rather than model self-assessment; the paper does not report the fallback rate.

method.core_idea: Adapt reliability engineering to agents by measuring repeated-run behavior, controlled perturbation response, self-assessed confidence, and harmful-policy compliance separately from task success.
method.mechanism: Run each agent-task pair five times; compare outcome and trace variability; rerun under paraphrased prompts, injected tool faults, and environment perturbations; elicit confidence and score calibration and selective prediction; use GPT-4o for compliance and severity judging. Aggregate consistency, Brier predictability, and robustness into an overall reliability index while displaying safety separately. If numeric confidence parsing fails, substitute a harness heuristic based on execution error count.
assumptions: Five executions estimate behavior distributions well enough for comparative reliability analysis.
Generated paraphrases preserve task semantics and the selected perturbation severities approximate realistic variation.
The benchmark scaffold does not dominate the model-level reliability signal.
Self-reported confidence can be compared across providers despite differences in API and reasoning behavior.
The selected equal weights and robustness ratios are meaningful across tasks with different baseline success rates.
The judge-generated severity score and the paper's three-band remapping provide a stable measure of operational harm despite their inconsistent category boundaries.
Confidence-parser fallbacks are rare enough that the error-count heuristic does not materially drive predictability results.

techniques.role: Estimates outcome, trajectory, action-sequence, and resource stability over five executions.
Tests prompt, tool-fault, and environment robustness relative to unperturbed success.
Measures calibration, discrimination, Brier error, and selective abstention from post-hoc agent self-assessments, with an error-count fallback on parse failure.
Scores policy compliance and harm severity on unsafe or conflicting requests.
Recomputes results on a corrected tau-bench subset to expose sensitivity to task validity.
Maps known production incidents onto proposed reliability dimensions as a face-validity check.

evaluations.setting: Fifteen agent models released over roughly 24 months on the 165-task GAIA validation set and the verified 26-task tau-bench airline subset.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy plus aggregate and dimension-level reliability.
evaluations.result: Accuracy rises faster than overall reliability; consistency and prompt robustness remain substantial differentiators among high-capability agents.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier model releases and unperturbed task success under the same benchmark scaffold.

evaluations.setting: Five repeated executions per agent-task pair.
evaluations.metric: Outcome, trajectory-distribution, action-sequence, and resource consistency.
evaluations.result: Agents with similar average task success can have materially different repeatability, and scale does not monotonically improve consistency.
evaluations.baseline: Mean task success, which collapses repeated-run variability.

evaluations.setting: Five GPT-4o paraphrases, tool faults injected at probability 0.2, and medium-strength environment perturbations.
evaluations.metric: Perturbed-to-baseline success ratios for prompt, fault, and environment robustness.
evaluations.result: Prompt robustness provides useful separation, while some perturbation scores exhibit ceiling or baseline-ratio effects.
evaluations.baseline: Original prompt and fault-free, unmodified environment.

evaluations.setting: Agent self-confidence on GAIA and cleaned tau-bench.
evaluations.metric: Expected calibration error, AUROC, Brier score, and selective-prediction behavior.
evaluations.result: Calibration improves across model generations, but tau-bench agents remain severely overconfident and selective abstention is close to random for many systems.
evaluations.baseline: Perfect calibration and random ranking of correct versus incorrect answers.

evaluations.metric: Changes in success, predictability, and safety after task removal.
evaluations.result: Cleaning improves accuracy, predictability, and safety for many agents, while consistency and robustness do not improve reliably, demonstrating that benchmark validity is part of reliability validity.

evaluations.setting: GPT-4o trace judging on the verified tau-bench airline subset.
evaluations.metric: Constraint compliance, conditional harm severity, and aggregate safety.
evaluations.result: Newer frontier models have lower violation rates; incorrect charges or refunds are the most common violation category, most violations are low-to-moderate, and rare high-severity cases remain.
evaluations.baseline: Older model releases evaluated with the same judge prompts and domain constraints.

limitations: Author-stated: two benchmarks and one scaffold per benchmark do not span the diversity of production agent systems.
Author-stated: metric definitions and equal-weight aggregation are a working operationalization rather than a universal definition of reliability.
Author-stated: safety is reported separately and a reliable system is not necessarily aligned or safe.
Author-stated: temperature-zero runs may overestimate repeatability relative to ordinary deployments.
Reviewer inference: robustness ratios become unstable or dominated by the epsilon convention as baseline task success approaches zero and saturate under the chosen weak perturbations.
Reviewer inference: static public benchmarks leave pretraining contamination unresolved; benchmark cleaning addresses label defects but not memorization.
Reviewer inference: provider, model, scaffold, API, reasoning-default, and compute changes are not factorially separated, so longitudinal model claims are partially confounded.
Reviewer inference: five inference repeats do not estimate training-seed uncertainty or rare catastrophic failures.
Reviewer inference: the fault wrapper's built-in probabilistic recovery partly determines the measured fault score.
Reviewer inference: the severity bands used for metric computation conflict with the labels shown to the judge and can down-weight prompt-labelled medium, high, and critical cases.
Reviewer inference: an unreported fraction of confidence scores comes from an error-count fallback rather than the agent's self-assessment.
failure_modes: An always-failing agent can score perfectly on outcome consistency, so reliability dashboards can be misread without capability alongside them.
A low-success baseline can inflate or destabilize perturbed-to-baseline robustness ratios.
Recovery logic in a fault-injection wrapper can be credited to the agent.
An LLM-generated paraphrase can subtly change task semantics and create artificial prompt fragility.
A shared LLM safety judge can reproduce provider biases or miss harms without an independent human audit.
Aggregate reliability can rise while safety worsens because safety is excluded from the aggregate.
A static benchmark can reward memorized task patterns while appearing consistent and calibrated.
A malformed confidence response can be replaced by the harness's error-count heuristic and make a predictability metric partly self-fulfilling.
The mismatched severity thresholds can make an operationally identical judged score receive a lower weight than its prompt-level label implies.
reusable_insights: Report capability, repeatability, perturbation robustness, calibration, and safety as a vector before considering any aggregate.
Attach an explicit operational profile, exposure unit, and failure definition to every agent reliability claim.
Validate perturbation semantics and automated judges on held-out human-rated samples.
Separate agent recovery from environment-wrapper recovery in fault-injection tests.
Treat benchmark defect audits and live or private task splits as components of reliability measurement.
Use prospective failure prediction, not retrospective incident mapping alone, to validate whether a reliability score has operational value.
open_questions: Which reliability dimensions predict costly production incidents on genuinely unseen deployments?
How should consistency be conditioned on task success so that repeatable failure is not mistaken for desirable reliability?
Can reliability estimates be made sample-efficient enough to detect rare failures without impractical repeated runs?
How should safety enter a deployment decision without being hidden by compensation from other dimensions?
Which perturbation distributions match real operational exposure rather than benchmark convenience?
How much measured reliability belongs to the model, scaffold, tool implementation, or surrounding recovery system?
What fraction of confidence responses invoke the error-count fallback, and how do predictability results change when those cases are excluded?
Which severity thresholds were intended—the category bands in the judge prompt or the different three-band mapping used in metric computation?

competitive_landscape.title: ReliabilityBench: Evaluating LLM Agent Reliability Under Production-Like Stress Conditions
competitive_landscape.difference: ReliabilityBench emphasizes pass^k consistency, environmental perturbations, and chaos-style fault injection over 1,280 production-like episodes; this paper covers more conceptual dimensions and models but uses a narrower benchmark and stress surface.

competitive_landscape.title: tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
competitive_landscape.difference: tau-bench introduces interactive tool-user tasks and pass^k consistency; this paper consumes and cleans it, then adds trace, perturbation, confidence, and safety dimensions.

competitive_landscape.title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
competitive_landscape.difference: The Holistic Agent Leaderboard factors model, scaffold, and benchmark across 21,730 runs and audits logs; this paper offers richer reliability metrics but does not factorially separate those axes.

competitive_landscape.title: Do Large Language Model Benchmarks Test Reliability?
competitive_landscape.difference: This study measures label and task errors and argues for platinum evaluation sets; it directly supports the present paper's cleaning sensitivity while showing that metric breadth cannot repair invalid ground truth.

competitive_landscape.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: AgentBench evaluates 27 models across eight interactive environments and analyzes capability failures; it does not decompose repeated-run reliability, calibration, and controlled perturbation response.

competitive_landscape.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
competitive_landscape.difference: GAIA supplies real-world assistant questions and capability scoring used here; the reliability framework adds repeated execution, perturbations, confidence, and safety around it.

competitive_landscape.title: Larger and more instructable language models become less reliable
competitive_landscape.difference: The Nature study shows larger, more instructable models can become less reliable across difficulty and prompt conditions; this paper extends the non-monotonic scale concern to tool-using agents with trace, fault, and confidence measures.

competitive_landscape.title: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Limited LLM Benchmark
competitive_landscape.difference: LiveBench uses frequently refreshed questions and objective scoring to limit contamination; the present evaluation remains static and addresses known task errors rather than memorization leakage.

competitive_landscape.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: AgentHarm provides 110 malicious agent tasks and 440 augmentations for dedicated harmfulness evaluation; this paper uses a smaller judge-based safety dimension and excludes it from overall reliability.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper proposes a science of agent reliability that unifies consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety and applies it longitudinally to contemporary tool-using agents.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It operationalizes twelve metrics, repeats runs across 15 models on GAIA and a verified 26-task tau-bench airline subset, adds three perturbation families and self-confidence evaluation, and shows capability gains can outpace reliability gains. The strongest negative results are saturated fault/environment scores and near-random tau-bench selective prediction.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful novelty is the multidimensional measurement vocabulary and shared protocol, not a validated deployment score. ReliabilityBench, tau-bench, AgentHarm, and earlier reliability work cover much of the component space; the aggregation is subjective, safety is excluded, evaluator independence is incomplete, the severity thresholds conflict, confidence can come from a harness fallback, and prospective production validity remains untested.

reviewer_notes: Independently reviewed the complete current target revision arXiv:2602.16666v3 from the indexed 52-page PDF: main text pages 1–9, references and appendix roadmap pages 10–15, Appendices A–E pages 16–27, the complete experimental protocol in Appendix F pages 27–36, and every extended result and figure in Appendix G pages 37–52. Concrete repairs made during this audit: corrected the evaluated tau-bench population to the verified 26-task airline subset (not airline plus retail), replaced obsolete appendix section labels in the anchors, added explicit null/negative results through Figures 17–20, recorded the page-36 severity-band contradiction and page-34 confidence fallback, corrected LiveBench's current title, and pinned every competitor to an exact primary-source revision or publisher record. Source provenance remains exactly index-derived. Official arXiv and Nature records were checked on 2026-08-23; the audit treats five runs as inference repeats, not model-training seeds, and does not infer causal scale trends from provider-confounded release chronology. Confidence is reduced from near-certainty because closed-provider behavior, paraphrase equivalence, judge validity, confidence-fallback frequency, and rare-event safety are not independently auditable from the paper.
